before: HashSet<int> represents a set of distinct integers. Adding an already-present value does not create another copy.
Add returns true when the set gains a new member, and false when the member was already present.
A set has no list-style index and should not be used when your result depends on a promised iteration order. Choose a list when ordered positions are part of your task.
Expected behavior from this example: False then 1. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Track repeated numeric IDs and compare attempts with distinct Count. Predict Add’s Boolean for each attempt. You may trace it on paper if no C# toolchain is installed; reading completion does not certify a run.
after: A set is a collection with no duplicate members. HashSet<int> holds distinct whole numbers: each number appears at most once.
Add tries to put a value into the set. If that value is already present, the set keeps just one copy.
Add returns true when it adds a new member. It returns false when the value was already there.
Count tells you how many different values are in the set. It does not count how many times Add was called.
The program prints False, then 1. The first call adds 4. The second call finds 4 already there, so the set still has one member.
Contains checks whether a value is in the set without changing it. A set has no numbered list positions or promised visiting order. Use a list when those positions matter.

before.question: Change only the second Add argument to 7. What changes?
choices: It still returns false because the set has one value already.
It removes 4 to make room for 7.
It returns true and Count becomes 2.
before.explanation: 7 is a new member, so the set grows while retaining 4.

after.question: Change only the second Add argument to 7. What happens?
choices: Add returns false because the set is not empty.
Add returns true and Count becomes 2.
after.explanation: 7 is new, so the set now contains both 4 and 7.
